items.note: Bhoj described as a peerless patron of poets and artists; five hundred scholars enjoyed his patronage; the Vagdevi image made by sculptor Manathala in Samvat 1091 (1034 CE).
Myths relating to Bhoj are abundant; Bhoj called the finest example of a history-person becoming a myth.
Gangeyadeva had humiliated and killed Munj; per the Prabandha-chintamani Bhoj attacked and won; Parijata-manjari mentions a Gangeyadeva-bhangotsava.
Proverb 'Where is King Bhoj, and where is Gangu the oilman' explained as a folk corruption of Gangeyadeva Telang.
Bhoj said to have erected the iron pillar at Dhar on the victory over Gangeyadeva Telang; later broken when removal was attempted.
Folk belief at Dhar that the huge stones and iron pillar sections near the Lat Masjid are the oilwoman's weights and balance-beam.
According to the Rasamala Gangeya fought Bhoj, was defeated and died at Prayag in 1041 CE; Bhoj erected a victory-pillar; towns such as Bhopal, Bhojpur and Bhopawar are said to be named after him.
The proverb is held to contain history, indicating Bhoj's successive victories over Gangeyadeva and Tailapa of Telangana.
Jayasi's Padmavat (1540 CE) calls Bhoj a knower of all fourteen branches of learning.
Current verse tying Dhar to the Paramaras: 'Where the Paramara, there Dhar.'
Merutunga's Prabandha-chintamani, written in the fourteenth century at Vardhamanapura, has Bhoj stories many of which are considered historical.
Bhoj called a supreme connoisseur of poetry; Bhoj II of the 13th century described in the Hammira-mahakavya as 'Bhoj, another like Bhoj'.
Prabandha-chintamani account of Bhoj's ancestors obtaining Malwa: Bhumada donated Malwa to Mahakaleshvara and appointed the Paramara family as protector.
Per this story the Paramaras were once protection-officers of Mahakal's Malava region; full sovereignty attained by Munj and conferred supreme glory by Bhoj.
Bhoj's dominance extended from Kannauj and Bhojpur in the north to the Tungabhadra in the south; he also defeated the Turushkas.
Bhoj's sons known from folk-tales: Vatsaraja (confirmed by the copper-plate of 1010), Devaraja, Phulkumar and Viranarayana.
